I've found relevant information about GitHub's fork management features. Here are the key findings:

## Detaching a Fork (Leaving the Fork Network)

To detach a fork, scroll down to the "Danger Zone" section in repository settings and click "Leave fork network". When you leave the fork network, the new repository will no longer automatically sync with changes from the original repository.

Leaving the fork network is permanent and the new repository cannot be reconnected to the fork network. Additionally, the new repository will not retain any of its issues, pull requests, wikis, stars, watchers, comments, child forks, or other metadata, though all git commit metadata will be preserved.

## Making a Forked Repository Private

Forks inherit the visibility of the original repository, and by default, public repositories can only be forked as public repositories. This is a GitHub limitation—you cannot directly make a public fork private through normal settings.

However, if you need to have a private version of a forked repository, you can manually create a new private repository and then clone the forked repository to your local machine, making it a separate private repository.

## Alternative Approach

For those seeking private forks of public repositories, a common workaround involves creating a bare clone and mirror-pushing it to a new private repository on GitHub, though this disconnects it from the fork network entirely.

content.text:
You can't do it directly because forks inherit their network's visibility — a fork of a public repo can't be made private while it's still in that network. Nothing about spinor specifically; it's structural.

Three ways out, and one is clearly right for you.

## Option A — Leave the fork network, then make it private *(recommended)*

This is now self-serve: **Settings → General → Danger Zone → "Leave fork network"**. It converts spinor into a standalone repo, after which the visibility toggle unlocks.

The three prerequisites, checked against your repo:

| Requirement | spinor |
|---|---|
| Must be public | ✓ public |
| Under 1 GB | ✓ 16.4 MB |
| No child forks | ✓ 0 forks |

You qualify on all three.

**What it destroys:** issues, pull requests, wikis, stars, watchers, comments, child forks. Git commit metadata is fully preserved. So I checked what you'd actually be giving up:

- **True issues: 0** (the API's count of 4 was all PRs)
- **Stars: 0, watchers: 0, child forks: 0**
- **Pull requests: 4** — #2, #3, #4 merged, **#1 still open**

So the entire real cost is four PR pages. The *code* from the merged three is on `main` and unaffected. **Merge PR #1 first** and the loss reduces to historical review discussion — and since branches survive as git refs, even an unmerged #1 could just be re-opened afterwards.

It's permanent; you can't rejoin the network later. That seems fine — you've said hasToggle.dev is becoming a Next.js playground and spinor is the product, so the fork relationship is already vestigial.

**One thing to verify after, not before:** the docs describe the result as "the new repository," which is ambiguous about whether the repo ID is preserved. If it isn't, your Actions secrets and the `spinor-renovate` App installation may not carry over. I couldn't determine that from the documentation, so don't assume either way — just re-check:

```sh
gh secret list --repo hasToggle/spinor
gh api /orgs/hasToggle/installations --jq '.installations[].app_slug'
gh workflow run renovate.yml -f dryRun=true   # end-to-end proof
```

## Option B — Mirror into a fresh private repo

The classic approach: `git clone --bare`, then `git push --mirror` to a new private repo. It loses the same PRs *and* changes the URL, so you'd re-link the Vercel project, re-install the App, re-add secrets, and re-point this Conductor workspace's remote. Strictly more work than A. Only worth it if you want to keep a public spinor around alongside the private one.

## Option C — Stay public

Worth weighing, because going private isn't free. **Actions minutes are unlimited on public repos and metered on private ones.** Your org is on the **Free** plan. Your Renovate runner is every 4 hours at ~1.5–2 min per run — roughly 350–400 minutes/month, plus whatever `claude.yml` uses. GitHub Free includes 2,000 private-repo minutes/month, so you'd be comfortably inside it, but I couldn't query your actual quota (the billing endpoint moved and needs `admin:org`), so confirm on your billing page rather than taking my number.

If the motivation is that the knowledge-hub product shouldn't be public, A is worth it regardless. If it's just tidiness, C is free.

## My recommendation

Merge PR #1, then Option A. It's one click, you lose essentially nothing measurable, and it removes the fork relationship that's already causing friction — recall `forkProcessing: "enabled"` in `renovate.json` and `gh repo set-default` being ambiguous. Both of those exist *only* because spinor is a fork; after detaching, the `forkProcessing` line becomes a harmless no-op you can drop.

Want me to open a PR removing `forkProcessing` once you've detached? It should come after, not before — removing it while still a fork would make Renovate skip the repo entirely.

Sources: [Detaching a fork](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/working-with-forks/detaching-a-fork), [What happens to forks when a repository changes visibility](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/working-with-forks/what-happens-to-forks-when-a-repository-is-deleted-or-changes-visibility)

content.text:
Renovate isn't refusing — **"unavailable" means it has no replacement mapping**, which is different. It reads npm's `deprecated` field, but that's free-form prose. A replacement *PR* only happens when Renovate has a machine-readable rule, either from its built-in `replacements:` presets (which `config:recommended` pulls in via `replacements:all`) or from your own `packageRules`. None of these four have an entry, and nothing can parse *"please install `@zanreal/nemo`"* into a rule. So it flags and stops.

I checked all four against your tree, and unpacked the tarballs rather than trusting the registry text — which was necessary, because the react-email deprecation message is misleading boilerplate and my first two readings of it were both wrong.

## What each one actually needs

| Package | Where | Reality |
|---|---|---|
| `@clerk/types` | `packages/auth` devDep | **Zero imports anywhere. Delete it.** |
| `@react-email/preview-server` | `apps/email` dep | **Zero imports.** `react-email@6` CLI provides `email dev`. Delete it. |
| `@rescale/nemo` | `apps/web`, 1 import in `proxy.ts:10` | Rename to `@zanreal/nemo` — same version, `3.0.1` |
| `@react-email/components` | `packages/email` + `apps/email`, 4 templates | Import from `react-email` instead |

**Half of this is deleting dead weight.** `@clerk/types` and `@react-email/preview-server` appear in no source file at all — they're leftovers from the next-forge template. That's two of your four warnings gone with no migration.

**`@rescale/nemo`** is a pure rename: `@zanreal/nemo` publishes the identical `3.0.1`. One line in `apps/web/package.json`, one import in `proxy.ts`.

**`@react-email/components`** is the only real migration, and it's still small. React Email 6.0 unified every component and the render utils into the single `react-email` package — which is why `components`, `button`, `html`, `tailwind`, `heading`, `text`, `section` are *all* deprecated while `@react-email/render` is not. I verified `react-email@6.9.1`'s type entry exports all thirteen components your templates use (`Body, Button, Container, Head, Heading, Hr, Html, Img, Link, Preview, Section, Tailwind, Text`) and re-exports `@react-email/render`. So it's an import-source change in 4 template files, plus adding `react-email` to `packages/email` — `apps/email` already has `6.9.1` pinned.

Worth knowing: `@react-email/ui` is **not** the successor despite what the setup docs imply. I unpacked it — it's the preview web app (Next.js, sidebar, toolbar, json-editor), the replacement for `preview-server`, not for `components`.

## Why you shouldn't make Renovate do this

You *can* teach it:

```json
{ "matchPackageNames": ["@rescale/nemo"], "replacementName": "@zanreal/nemo", "replacementVersion": "3.0.1" }
```

But **Renovate replacement rules only rewrite manifests, never import statements.** That PR would set `@zanreal/nemo` in `package.json` while `proxy.ts` still imports `@rescale/nemo` — a broken build, auto-merged, with no CI to catch it given where your automerge config currently stands. Same for the react-email change across four templates.

So "unavailable" is arguably Renovate being honest: these need source edits it can't make. Do them by hand once and the dashboard section disappears.

## Want me to do it?

I'd split it three ways, smallest blast radius first:

1. **Delete the two unused deps** — manifest-only, nothing imports them, zero risk.
2. **`@rescale/nemo` → `@zanreal/nemo`** — touches `apps/web/proxy.ts`, your middleware. Verifiable with typecheck plus a `turbo build --filter=web`.
3. **`@react-email/components` → `react-email`** — touches 4 email templates. These render real customer email, so worth eyeballing in `email dev` (port 3003) before merging rather than trusting a typecheck.

Say the word and I'll start with 1 and 2, and hold 3 until you've had a chance to preview the templates. Or all three at once if you'd rather review them together.

Sources: [React Email 6.0 announcement](https://resend.com/blog/react-email-6), [React Email docs](https://react.email/docs/components/html), [Renovate replacement presets](https://docs.renovatebot.com/presets-replacements/)

content.text:
All four resolved — **PR #7: https://github.com/hasToggle/spinor/pull/7**

## One judgment call

I put this in **one PR with three commits** rather than three PRs. Each change touches `bun.lock`, so three parallel branches would have conflicted on it and needed sequential rebasing for no review benefit — you review locally anyway. The commits are cleanly separated, so any one can be reverted independently. Say the word if you'd rather I split them.

| Commit | Change |
|---|---|
| `13a2663` | delete `@clerk/types` + `@react-email/preview-server` — both unused |
| `fc79f04` | `@rescale/nemo` → `@zanreal/nemo` |
| `7f2017f` | `@react-email/components` → `react-email` |

## Verification

**The templates actually render.** `email export` produced all four HTML files — 5.5–6.2 KB each with real `<table>` markup. That's the check that counts: a typecheck passes on a component that resolves but fails at render time.

`turbo typecheck` is 22/24. The failure is `storybook#typecheck` — implicit-`any` in stories — which I confirmed produces **byte-identical errors on `origin/main`**. Pre-existing, unrelated.

`@zanreal/nemo` exports `createNEMO`, verified at runtime rather than assumed. Biome findings in the templates: 12 before, 12 after.

## Two corrections I had to make mid-work

Both came from reading the registry text instead of the packages, and both would have produced a broken PR:

**I first called the react-email deprecations spurious.** The message is npm's generic *"no longer supported"* boilerplate naming no successor — unlike `@clerk/types` and `@rescale/nemo`, which name theirs. But it's a real deprecation: React Email 6 consolidated all components plus render into `react-email`. The tell was that `@react-email/render` is *not* deprecated while every component package is.

**Then I nearly recommended `@react-email/ui` as the replacement**, because the setup docs list it. I unpacked the tarball: it's the preview *web app* — Next.js, sidebar, toolbar, JSON editor, and an `index.mjs` that exports only `version`. It replaces `preview-server`, not `components`. Had I shipped that, imports would have failed outright.

## Incidental findings

The `useSortedKeys` and `noRedundantDefaultExport` findings in `packages/email/keys.ts` and the templates predate this work — I left them alone, and used `--only=assist/source/organizeImports` so the necessary import reordering didn't sweep them in.

`@react-email/render` is still imported directly in `apps/app/.../digest/[id]/preview/page.tsx` and `apps/email/scripts/digest.ts`. It isn't deprecated so I left it, though `react-email` now re-exports it if you'd like to consolidate later.

Once this merges, the Deprecations / Replacements section of the dashboard should disappear on Renovate's next run.

name: Renovate

# Self-hosted replacement for the Mend Cloud Runner that drives hasToggle.dev.
# The bot identity is a GitHub App owned by the org (see docs/renovate.md);
# nothing here depends on a human's personal access token.

on:
  schedule:
    # Every four hours. This only controls how often Renovate wakes up and
    # looks — what it is allowed to open is decided by renovate.json.
    - cron: "0 */4 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      logLevel:
        description: Log level
        type: choice
        default: info
        options:
          - debug
          - info
          - warn
      dryRun:
        description: Dry run — resolve everything, write nothing
        type: boolean
        default: false

# Two overlapping runs duplicate branch work and can race each other's
# automerge step. Queue rather than cancel so a scheduled tick is never lost.
concurrency:
  group: renovate
  cancel-in-progress: false

# The job's own GITHUB_TOKEN does nothing here — every write goes through the
# App installation token minted below.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  renovate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Mint an App installation token
        id: app-token
        uses: actions/create-github-app-token@v3
        with:
          # client-id, not the numeric app-id: the latter is deprecated in v3.
          # Neither is actually secret — `gh api /apps/spinor-renovate` returns
          # the client id to anyone — but keeping it alongside the private key
          # keeps this step uniform.
          # actionlint reports client-id as an unknown input; its bundled action
          # metadata is stale. Verified against a real run instead.
          client-id: ${{ secrets.RENOVATE_APP_CLIENT_ID }}
          private-key: ${{ secrets.RENOVATE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          owner: ${{ github.repository_owner }}
          repositories: ${{ github.event.repository.name }}

      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          # Renovate clones the repo itself with the App token; the checkout is
          # only here to give the action a workspace. Leaving the Actions
          # credentials behind in .git/config would serve no purpose.
          persist-credentials: false

      # Setting the env var only when the input is true keeps RENOVATE_DRY_RUN
      # absent on normal runs — an empty string is not a valid dryRun value.
      - name: Enable dry run
        if: ${{ inputs.dryRun }}
        run: echo "RENOVATE_DRY_RUN=full" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Renovate
        uses: renovatebot/github-action@v46.2.0
        with:
          token: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token }}
          # Floats within the major so patches arrive without a config bump;
          # Renovate keeps the `uses:` pin above current by itself.
          renovate-version: 44
        env:
          # Global (self-hosted) config lives here rather than in a config file
          # so there is one place to read. The action forwards any RENOVATE_*
          # and LOG_LEVEL vars into the container.
          RENOVATE_PLATFORM: github
          RENOVATE_REPOSITORIES: ${{ github.repository }}
          # renovate.json is already committed, so the onboarding-PR flow is
          # dead weight — and requiring config means a run against a repo
          # without one fails loudly instead of silently doing nothing.
          RENOVATE_ONBOARDING: "false"
          RENOVATE_REQUIRE_CONFIG: required
          LOG_LEVEL: ${{ inputs.logLevel || 'info' }}
